_schema_notes.type_hard_bound: Eliminates impossible date ranges entirely. Model output is clipped to these bounds regardless of confidence.
_schema_notes.type_soft_anchor: Boosts probability toward a likely range but does not eliminate others. Used when exceptions exist.
_schema_notes.confidence: high = very few exceptions, medium = common rule with notable exceptions, low = weak signal or many exceptions
_schema_notes.likely_start: Start of the boosted probability range
_schema_notes.likely_end: End of the boosted probability range

China.notes: US-China trade normalization and manufacturing shift. Pre-1995 Chinese production for US market is essentially nonexistent in vintage clothing.

Hong Kong.notes: Peak Hong Kong garment export era. HK handover to China in 1997 began a manufacturing shift. Hard outer bound: HK as a distinct manufacturing origin largely disappears post-2000.

Korea.notes: South Korea was a major US garment supplier during this window. Rising labor costs pushed production out by the late 1990s.

Taiwan.notes: Same manufacturing era as Korea and HK. Taiwan's garment export to the US peaked in the 1980s-90s.

USA.notes: Domestic US production declined sharply through the 1990s-2000s due to NAFTA and trade liberalization. Post-2005 Made in USA is almost exclusively small indie or heritage brands whose identity is domestic production — these are exceptions, not the norm. A Made in USA label on a mass-market garment strongly suggests pre-2000.

Mexico.notes: NAFTA (1994) drove a significant wave of US production shifting to Mexico. Most Mexican-made American-market garments cluster in the late 1990s-2000s window.

El Salvador.notes: Central American garment production for US market grew post-NAFTA era. Weaker signal than Mexico — use in combination with other tells.

Honduras.notes: Same window as El Salvador. Central American production bloc.

Guatemala.notes: Same window as El Salvador and Honduras.

Bangladesh.notes: Bangladesh became a dominant low-cost garment exporter in the 1990s onward. Presence suggests post-1990 but is not a tight anchor.

West Germany.notes: West Germany ceased to exist as a political entity upon reunification in October 1990. Any garment labeled West Germany predates this.

East Germany.notes: Same reunification hard bound as West Germany.

Japan.notes: Japan was a significant US garment exporter in the late 1950s-1960s. Rising labor costs pushed production to cheaper markets by the mid-1970s. 'Made in Japan' on American-market clothing is a strong signal for 1955-1975.

Philippines.notes: Philippines became a significant US garment supplier from the mid-1970s onward as Japan became too expensive. Peak window 1975-1995.

India.notes: India's garment export to the US grew substantially from the 1980s onward. Presence suggests post-1980.

Sri_Lanka.notes: Sri Lanka developed as a garment export country in the 1980s. Presence suggests post-1980.

Vietnam.notes: US-Vietnam trade relations normalized with the US embargo lifting in 1994. 'Made in Vietnam' on US-market garments indicates post-1994, with significant volume beginning in 1995-1996.

Cambodia.notes: Cambodia's garment export to the US grew from the mid-1990s following trade agreements. Presence suggests post-1995.

Indonesia.notes: Indonesia became a major US garment supplier from the mid-1980s. Strongly associated with Nike and other sportswear brands.

Czechoslovakia.notes: Czechoslovakia dissolved into the Czech Republic and Slovakia on January 1, 1993. Any garment labeled 'Made in Czechoslovakia' or 'Czechoslovakia' predates 1993.

Romania.notes: Romania became a significant European garment manufacturer for Western markets after 1990. Presence suggests post-1990.

absent.notes: FTC Care Labeling Rule took effect July 3, 1971. All garments sold in the US after this date were required to include permanent care instructions. Absence of a care label is a hard ceiling of 1971.

present.notes: Presence of a care label does not itself date the garment beyond post-1971, but eliminates pre-1971.

absent.notes: Textile Fiber Products Identification Act passed 1960, effective 1960. Required fiber content disclosure on all textile products sold in the US.

screenprinted_collar.notes: A brand identifier screenprinted or heat-transferred directly onto the inside back collar (no physical tag) is almost exclusively a post-2005 practice. Driven by cost reduction and comfort trends in the mid-2000s fast fashion era. Seeing this on a garment is a strong signal it is not vintage in the traditional sense.

woven_tag.notes: Woven tags were standard across most of the 20th century. Presence alone is not a strong dating signal but is consistent with pre-2005 production.

paper_tag.notes: Paper hang tags and paper inner labels were more common in mid-century production. Placeholder — tag material dating is nuanced and should be refined with more specific examples.

tag_construction._todo: Tag shape, font style, and fabric/material of the physical tag are meaningful signals but require visual classification rather than rule-based treatment. These will be handled by the model's visual features, not this rules engine. Document specific examples here as they are identified during labeling.

rn_number._note: RN (Registered Number) and WPL (Wool Products Label) numbers are traceable to specific companies and registration dates via the FTC database. A garment cannot predate the registration year of its RN number. This is a hard bound — implement RN lookup as a separate module against the FTC registry.

wpl_present.notes: WPL numbers were issued under the Wool Products Label Act of 1939. The FTC stopped issuing WPL numbers in 1971 and switched to RN numbers, but existing WPL numbers stayed valid and many brands (Levi's WPL 423, Russell, others) kept printing them for decades. A WPL with no care label is pre-1971; a WPL alongside a care label is not a ceiling.

rn_present.notes: RN numbers were introduced by the FTC in 1952 under the Fur Products Labeling Act, then extended to all textile products. Presence of an RN number means the garment is post-1952 at the earliest. Higher RN numbers indicate later registration dates.

talon.notes: Talon was the dominant American zipper manufacturer for most of the 20th century. 'Talon' stamped on the pull or slider. Presence strongly suggests pre-1980 production on American garments. Talon lost significant market share to YKK through the 1970s and largely exited the apparel market.

talon_lightning.notes: The 'Lightning' brand was Talon's early zipper line. More specific than just 'Talon' — associated with 1930s-1950s garments.

conmar.notes: Conmar Products Corporation was an American zipper manufacturer active from the 1930s. Largely absorbed or displaced by the 1960s. 'Conmar' on the pull indicates pre-1965.

scovill.notes: Scovill Manufacturing made zippers (and snaps) under the 'Gripper' brand. Present on workwear and casual garments from the 1930s-1960s.

ykk.notes: YKK (Yoshida Kogyo Kabushikikaisha) began US operations approximately 1960 and became the dominant American market zipper by the mid-1970s. 'YKK' on the pull is a hard post-1960 indicator. On American vintage clothing, YKK presence strongly suggests post-1965.

crown.notes: Crown was an American zipper brand. Needs further documentation — flag for user verification.

gripper_scovill.notes: Scovill's 'Gripper' snaps are common on American workwear, western shirts, and outerwear. 'Gripper' or 'Scovill' stamped on snap. Associated with mid-20th century American production.

dot_snaps.notes: DOT brand snaps (also Scovill) appear on workwear and western shirts across a wide date range. Not a strong dating signal alone but can corroborate other evidence.

no_name_stamped_snaps.notes: Plain stamped metal snaps without brand marking are more common on earlier garments. Low signal on its own.

wash_n_wear.notes: 'Wash and Wear', 'Wash 'N Wear', or 'Wrinkle-Free' marketing copy on labels is associated with the synthetic fabric boom of the 1950s-1960s. These terms were heavily marketed before the FTC care label mandate made them redundant.

sanforized.notes: 'Sanforized' is a trademarked pre-shrinking process developed by Sanford Cluett, licensed from 1936. Common marketing term on denim and workwear labels through the mid-20th century. Fell out of label use as preshrinking became industry standard.

sanforized_plus.notes: 'Sanforized-Plus' (also 'Sanforized Plus-2') was a follow-up process for stretch fabrics introduced in the late 1960s.

drip_dry.notes: 'Drip Dry' copy on labels is associated with the synthetic/rayon garment era of the 1950s-1960s, before formal care label requirements.

size_without_state_country.notes: Older labels often show only the brand and size with no country of origin, care instructions, or fiber content. Absence of all regulatory info suggests pre-1960 production.

percent_symbol_fiber.notes: Percentage-based fiber content disclosure (e.g., '65% Polyester, 35% Cotton') is required by the Textile Fiber Products Identification Act of 1960. Presence confirms post-1960.

polyester_blend.notes: Commercial polyester (Dacron) was introduced to the US market in 1953. Any garment labeled as containing polyester postdates 1953. Polyester blends in mass-market clothing peaked 1965-1980.

dacron_label.notes: Dacron was DuPont's brand name for polyester fiber, heavily marketed as a label claim in the 1950s-1970s. By the 1980s, garments simply listed 'polyester' rather than the trade name.

nylon_label.notes: Nylon was introduced commercially in 1940. Any garment containing nylon is post-1940.

qiana.notes: Qiana was DuPont's luxury nylon brand, introduced 1968, heavily used in disco-era fashion. Fell out of use by the mid-1980s.

spandex_lycra.notes: Spandex (Lycra) introduced commercially by DuPont in 1962. Any garment labeled with spandex/Lycra content postdates 1962. Became common in activewear from the 1980s onward.

made_in_usa_no_qualifiers.notes: Plain 'Made in U.S.A.' with no additional manufacturing qualifiers is more common pre-NAFTA. Post-1994 FTC rules required 'Made in U.S.A.' to mean all or virtually all domestic content — some brands moved to qualified claims or stopped using it.

assembled_in_usa.notes: 'Assembled in U.S.A. of imported components' or similar qualified claims are post-1994 FTC rule era. Distinguishes from full domestic production.

single_stitch_hem.notes: Single-needle stitching on T-shirt sleeve and bottom hems is associated with pre-1994 production on American blanks (Fruit of the Loom, Hanes, Champion, etc.). Chain-stitch and double-needle hems became standard as brands moved offshore. One of the most reliable T-shirt dating signals.

selvedge_denim.notes: Selvedge (self-edge) denim from narrow-width shuttle looms was standard on American jeans until the 1960s-1980s when projectile looms producing wider non-selvedge denim became dominant. Selvedge visible on the inside seam of jeans strongly suggests pre-1985, and likely pre-1970s on major brands like Levi's.

chain_stitch_outseam.notes: Chain stitch on the outseam of jeans is a vintage production indicator. Major brands transitioned to lock stitch as production modernized in the late 1970s-early 1980s.

woolmark_present.notes: The Woolmark symbol (circular interlocked yarn ball design) was launched in August 1964 by the International Wool Secretariat. Any garment bearing the Woolmark symbol is post-1964.

woolblend_mark.notes: The Woolblend Mark was introduced in 1971 for garments made from wool blended with another fiber. Presence indicates post-1971.

symbols_only_no_words.notes: In December 1996 the USA adopted the ASTM D5489 care symbol system. Labels using only pictorial care symbols with no accompanying text are post-1996 by the new standard. Mixed symbol/text labels were common in the transition 1996-2005.

text_only_care_instructions.notes: Care instructions in text only (no symbols) were the standard from the 1971 FTC mandate through the 1990s. Text-only labels are consistent with 1971-1996, though some manufacturers continued text into the 2000s.

hand_wash_cold.notes: Instruction to hand wash cold is more common on vintage delicate garments and pre-machine-wash-era instructions. Low signal on its own.

dsa_contract_prefix.notes: US military contracts prefixed 'DSA' (Defense Supply Agency) were issued 1962-1977. DSA was renamed DLA (Defense Logistics Agency) in 1977. A DSA contract number on a military garment brackets it to 1962-1977.

dla_contract_prefix.notes: DLA (Defense Logistics Agency) contract prefix used from 1977 onward.

military_date_code.notes: US military contract labels contain a two-digit date code within the contract number representing the fiscal year the contract was awarded. This is a direct manufacturing date indicator. Note: contract award year may precede garment production by up to 1-2 years in some cases.

m65_field_jacket.notes: The M-65 Field Jacket was introduced in 1965 to replace the M-51. Any M-65 labeled garment is post-1965.

m51_field_jacket.notes: The M-51 Field Jacket was introduced in 1951 and phased out by 1968 when M-65 production was fully established.

ginetex_symbols.notes: GINETEX care symbols (used internationally, especially on European-origin garments) date to 1963 when the organization was founded. ISO 3758 standard first published 1991.
